results.proof_sketch: Suppose p zombies guarantee capture within t rounds. Their initial radius-t neighborhoods must cover every possible initial survivor vertex: otherwise the survivor can start outside their union and remain stationary, and no zombie can traverse the initial distance in t moves. An L1-ball of radius t is contained in an L∞ cube of size at most (2t+1)^k, so n^k≤p(2t+1)^k. Put x=p+t. Since p≥1, p≤x and 2t+1≤3x; hence n^k≤3^k x^(k+1). Thus p+t≥3^(-k/(k+1))n^(k/(k+1)). This holds for every admissible p, so minimizing p+capt_z(G,p) proves the claim.

results.claim: Mesh capture lemma: for each r≥1 there are constants M_r,A_r such that, on every r-dimensional Cartesian grid with coordinate meshes containing both endpoints and having gaps at most d, placing M_r zombies at every mesh intersection guarantees capture in at most A_r d rounds.
results.proof_sketch: Set M_1=A_1=1. In one dimension a survivor starting off the mesh is bracketed by zombies at consecutive mesh points, and their separation contracts until capture within d rounds; a survivor on the mesh is captured initially. Inductively set M_r=2rM_{r-1}, A_r=(r+1)(A_{r-1}+1), and R=A_{r-1}d. For each coordinate i and each side of the survivor, use the boundary hyperplane if it is within R; otherwise the gap condition supplies a mesh hyperplane at distance in [R,R+d). Assign a disjoint projected (r−1)-dimensional team to each of these 2r labeled hyperplanes. Its moves in non-i coordinates reduce the full L1 distance and are legal zombie moves. Within R rounds each team supplies an i-guard matching the survivor outside coordinate i. A nonboundary plane cannot be crossed strictly in R moves. If it is reached on the last move, that move either encounters an already aligned guard or changes coordinate i and therefore cannot newly create a projected alignment; boundaries cannot be crossed. An established guard repairs the unique projected mismatch from the preceding survivor move, or advances in coordinate i when already aligned, so it remains on its assigned side. One additional zombie turn synchronizes all guards. Let W be the sum of the r lower-to-upper guard separations. Initially W<2r(R+d). After a survivor move in coordinate j, the j-guards advance and reduce W by 2 while all other guards repair coordinate j; after a stay every pair advances. Thus each noncapture round reduces W by at least 2, giving capture within r(R+d) further rounds. Finally R+1+r(R+d)≤A_rd for integral d≥1. Degenerate coordinates only cause earlier capture.

results.claim: Consequently, for every fixed k≥3, th_z((P_n)^{□k})=Θ_k(n^{k/(k+1)})=Θ_k(|G|^{1/(k+1)}); in particular the k=3 endpoint is complete.
results.proof_sketch: Use the endpoint-augmented coordinate mesh {0,d,2d,…}∪{n−1}. Its gaps are at most d and it has at most n/d+2 points, so the mesh lemma supplies p≤M_k(n/d+2)^k zombies and capture time at most A_kd. Taking d=⌈n^(k/(k+1))⌉ makes both quantities O_k(n^(k/(k+1))). For sufficiently large n this placement has p≤n^k; the finitely many smaller n are handled by occupying every vertex and absorbed into the fixed-k constant. The first claim supplies the matching lower bound. Since |G|=n^k, n^(k/(k+1))=|G|^(1/(k+1)). The recurrences give M_2=4, A_2=6, M_3=24, and A_3=28, explicitly covering k=3.

final_writeup:
The answer is affirmative for every fixed k≥3.

Let G_{n,k}=(P_n)^{□k}, represented by {0,…,n−1}^k with L1 adjacency, so |G_{n,k}|=n^k.

For the lower bound, suppose p zombies guarantee capture within t rounds. Their initial radius-t neighborhoods must cover the grid: otherwise a survivor can start outside every such neighborhood and remain stationary, and no zombie can reach it in t moves. Each radius-t L1-ball has at most (2t+1)^k vertices, giving

n^k≤p(2t+1)^k.

Writing x=p+t, we have p≤x and, because p≥1, 2t+1≤3x. Hence n^k≤3^k x^(k+1), and every throttling strategy satisfies

p+t≥3^(-k/(k+1))n^(k/(k+1)).

For the upper bound, use the following mesh lemma. In dimension r, let every coordinate have a mesh containing both endpoints and with gaps at most d. Define

M_1=A_1=1,  M_r=2rM_{r−1},  A_r=(r+1)(A_{r−1}+1).

Placing M_r zombies at every mesh intersection guarantees capture within A_rd rounds.

For r=1, a survivor off the mesh is bracketed by zombies at consecutive mesh points. It cannot cross either zombie, and their separation contracts until capture within d rounds. Starting on a mesh point causes immediate capture.

Assume the lemma in dimension r−1 and put R=A_{r−1}d. For every coordinate i, select a mesh hyperplane on each side of the survivor. Use the boundary if it is within R; otherwise the mesh-gap condition supplies a hyperplane at distance in [R,R+d). On each of these 2r labeled hyperplanes, assign a disjoint team of M_{r−1} zombies per mesh intersection and run the dimension-(r−1) strategy against the survivor's projection obtained by deleting coordinate i. Every projected zombie move changes a mismatching coordinate toward the survivor, so it is also a legal full-grid shortest-path move.

Within R rounds each team produces an i-guard agreeing with the survivor in every coordinate except possibly i. A selected nonboundary hyperplane cannot be crossed strictly within R survivor moves. If the survivor reaches it on the last move, then either the guard was already aligned or that move changes coordinate i and leaves the projection unchanged; in either case crossing causes capture. A boundary cannot be crossed.

Maintain an established i-guard by repairing the unique projected mismatch created by the preceding survivor move or, if no such mismatch exists, advancing toward the survivor in coordinate i. The guard therefore remains on its assigned side. The multiplicity M_r=2rM_{r−1} supplies disjoint teams even where several selected hyperplanes meet. After one additional zombie turn all lower and upper guards are simultaneously aligned.

Let W be the sum, over all coordinates, of the separations between the corresponding lower and upper guards. The selected hyperplanes initially have separation less than 2(R+d), and guards only move inward before synchronization, so W<2r(R+d). If the survivor moves in coordinate j, then on the next zombie turn the two j-guards advance inward, reducing W by 2, while every other guard repairs coordinate j. If the survivor stays, every guard pair advances. Thus every noncapture round reduces W by at least 2, and capture follows within r(R+d) further rounds. The total is at most

R+1+r(R+d)≤(r+1)(A_{r−1}+1)d=A_rd,

where the inequality uses d≥1. This proves the mesh lemma. Degenerate coordinates only make capture occur earlier.

For G_{n,k}, take the endpoint-augmented mesh {0,d,2d,…}∪{n−1} in every coordinate. It has gaps at most d and at most n/d+2 points per coordinate. Therefore the strategy uses at most M_k(n/d+2)^k zombies and captures within A_kd rounds. With d=⌈n^(k/(k+1))⌉, both terms are O_k(n^(k/(k+1))). For all sufficiently large n the number of zombies is at most n^k; any remaining finite cases are handled by initially occupying every vertex.

Combining the bounds gives

th_z(G_{n,k})=Θ_k(n^(k/(k+1)))=Θ_k(|G_{n,k}|^(1/(k+1))).

For k=3, the recurrences give M_3=24 and A_3=28, so one explicit strategy uses at most 24(n/d+2)^3 zombies and capture time at most 28d with d=⌈n^(3/4)⌉. Thus the requested k=3 endpoint, and indeed every fixed k≥3, is complete.
